title: Life cycle assessment of copper production- a case study in China
section: of refined copper was higher than that of reclaimed copper in almost all categories except for human toxicity because of the direct atmospheric arsenic emission during the copper recycling stage. The overall environmental impact for the refined copper production was mainly attributed to metal depletion, freshwa- ter ecotoxicity, marine ecotoxicity, and water depletion potential impact. By contrast, that for the reclaimed copper production was mainly caused by human toxicity impact. Conclusions Results show that the reclaimed copper scenario had approximately 59 to 99% more environmental benefits than those of the refined copper scenario in most key catego- ries except for human toxicity, in which a similar environmen- tal burden was observed between both scenarios. The key factors that reduce the overall environmental impact for China ' s copper industry include decreasing direct heavy metal emissions in air and water, increasing the national recycling rate of copper, improving electricity consumption efficiency, replacing coal with clean energy sources for electricity pro- duction, and optimizing the efficiency of copper ore mining and consumption. Keywords Environmental benefit . Life cycle assessment . Refined copper . Reclaimed copper . Regional level 1 Introduction With the rapid economic and industrial development of China, the production of refined copper products consistently in- creased during the last decade (China Statistical Yearbook 2005 - 2015) from approximately 2.04 million tons in 2004 to 7.96 million tons in 2014, thereby indicating an average annual increase of 14.58%. According to statistical data, China is the world ' s largest producer of refined and reclaimed copper, which account for 31.48 and 58.12%, respectively, of the total global output in 2013 (China Statistical Yearbook 2014 ; Wang et al. 2015 ). However, China, which is also the world ' s largest consumer of copper, faces numerous chal- lenges. The Chinese copper industry suffers from low electric- ity efficiency and copper recovery rate, as well as the overuse of raw materials (HJ 559-2010 2010 ). Moreover, pollutants, such as particulates, SO 2 , CO 2 , NO 2 , solid waste, and wastewater, which are gen- erated from copper manufacturing processes, may seriously damage the environment and the health of the population of neighboring areas . Copper, which is a nonrenewable resource, is crucial in eco- nomic development. Therefore, systematically evaluating the environmental impacts of copper production in China is cru- cial to identify key factors in the industrial life cycle that may alleviate the shortage of copper resources, reduce the energy consumption, and decrease environmental pollution. Life cycle assessment (LCA) is a beneficial tool to assess the environmental impacts of products, processes, or activities generated during their entire life cycles. The environmental impacts of the copper industry are extensively studied world- wide . However, most previous studies only focused on several im- pact categories  and failed to collect actual field data on direct water and air emissions. Moreover, studies (Song et al. 2014 ; Streicher-Porte and Althaus 2010 ; Li and Guan 2009 ) that have employed the LCA approach on copper production in China are limited in international peer-reviewed journals. Song et al. ( 2014 ) studied the environmental burdens in China from copper production. However, a percentage of the inventory data of this research were obtained from the GaBi database, thereby possibly leading to inaccurate results because of the differences in energy structures and technolo- gies between China and Europe. Similarly, Streicher-Porte and Althaus ( 2010 ) reported a LCA study of copper produc- tion in China on the basis of reported Chinese industry data between 2006 and 2009 and ecoinvent database. No wastes such as slag, filter ashes, dusts, and sludge were involved. Li and Guan ( 2009 ) presented a conference article on the process of recycling copper based on the LCA method. However, their data sources and key factors were unclear (ISO 14040 2006a , b ); both the energy input and pollution output information were inaccurate in their study. Furthermore, no study per- formed a sensitivity or uncertainty analysis. Thus, the results were unreliable. To solve these problems, an LCA of copper production in China was conducted. The goals of the current study were to quantify and compare the environmental im- pacts of refined and reclaimed copper production, identify their key factors, explore potential methods for environmental improvements, and determine the level of confidence in the assertion that reclaimed copper is more environment-friendly than refined copper. 2 Scope definition 2.1 Functional unit The functional unit provides a quantified reference for all re- lated inputs and outputs of a product. In this study, the pro- duction of 1 ton of copper (i.e., refined or reclaimed copper) was selected as the functional unit. All raw materials and energy consumption, road transport, direct emissions (i.e., air pollutants, wastewater emission, and solid waste genera- tion), and waste disposal management were based on this functional unit. 2.2 System boundary System boundaries were established by applying a cradle-to- gate approach for two scenarios, namely, the refined and reclaimed copper scenarios (Fig. 1 ). The former began with copper ore mining, whereas the latter started from old copper collection. Each of the processes considered raw materials and energy consumption, road transportation, direct pollutant emissions, and waste disposal. In particular, the industrial waste gangue generated from mining was dealt with the stor- age method, solid waste from copper refining and slag pro- duced from copper reclaiming were reused as building mate- rials, and waste refractory matter and anode were recycled. By contrast, other solid and hazardous wastes, including arsenic residues generated from copper refining or reclaiming, were disposed via sanitary landfills. 2.3 LCIA methodology A life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) was conducted at the midpoint level by employing the ReCiPe method, which is one of the most commonly used indicator approaches in the LCA analysis . This method was built on the results of Eco-indicator 99 (Goedkoop and Spriensma 2001 ) and Centrum voor Milieukunde Leiden (i.e., CML 2000) (Guinée et al. 2001 ) with some modifications on LCA. The ReCiPe approach defines 18 midpoint categories: climate change, ozone depletion, human toxicity, photochemical oxidant formation, particulate matter formation, ionizing radiation, terrestrial acidification, freshwater eutrophication, marine eutrophication, terrestrial ecotoxicity, freshwater ecotoxicity, marine ecotoxicity, agri- cultural land occupation, urban land occupation, natural land transformation, water depletion, metal depletion, and fossil depletion. Particularly, potential environmental effects of future extractions are included in the LCIA results. In addition, normalization which is determined by the ratio of the impact per unit of emission divided by the per capita world impact for the year 2000 (Wegener Sleeswijk et al. 2008 ) was applied in this study to analyze the respective share of each midpoint Int J Life Cycle Assess impact to the overall impact as well as to present comparable midpoint impacts. Detailed methodology and characteriza- tion factors of the ReCiPe model are available on the website of Institute of Environmental Science at Leiden University in the Netherlands ( http://www.cml.leiden. edu/research/industrialecology/research projects/finished/ recipe.html ). Uncertainty analysis was conducted based on Monte-Carlo simulation. The LCI data presented in this study were collected from two refined and reclaimed copper production sites in China. Mass allocation regarding all the inputs and outputs of refined copper scenario is performed in this study. The annual capacities for refined copper using double side blowing bath smelting technology and reclaimed copper were approximately 130 and 35 kt, re- spectively, in 2014. The copper content rate of copper ore and copper concentrate is around 0.8 and 23.7%, respectively. The heavy metals (i.e., lead, copper, arsenic, and zinc) and sulfur content rates of refined copper scenario are shown in Table 2 . The reviewed LCI in China for the national average coal- based electricity generation , road transpor- tation , municipal solid waste disposal , hazardous waste , and wastewater treatment  were applied in the current study. The data on chemicals, natural gas, and heavy fuel oil production in Europe (Ecoinvent centre 2015 ) were adopted because of lack of information in China. To reduce the regionalized effect from Europe, the Chinese data on the aforementioned national coal-based electricity genera- tion  and road transport  were used to adjust the European data to the Chinese situation. The LCA was conducted using the SimaPro 8.2 software. 3 Results and discussion 3.1 LCIA results Table 3 compares the LCIA results for both refined and reclaimed copper scenarios. The environmental impact of re- fined copper was higher than that of reclaimed copper in almost all categories except for human toxicity and natural land trans- formation. In particular, the impact of refined copper was sub- stantially higher (i.e., almost or over 10 times) on freshwater eutrophication, terrestrial ecotoxicity, freshwater ecotoxicity, agricultural land occupation, and metal depletion than that of the reclaimed copper industry. For ozone depletion and natural land transformation, the two scenarios had similar impacts. Furthermore, the normalized LCIA midpoint scores for the entire life cycle in each scenario (Fig. 2 ) indicated that the environmental impact of the refined copper production indus- try was considerably higher than that of the reclaimed copper industry. In the refined copper scenario, metal depletion, freshwater ecotoxicity, marine ecotoxicity, and fossil deple- tion were the dominant contributors to the overall environ- mental impacts. Climate change, terrestrial acidification, freshwater and marine eutrophication, human toxicity, photo- chemical oxidant formation, particulate matter formation, and terrestrial ecotoxicity had minor to medium contributions, whereas the other impact categories could be disregarded. However, for the reclaimed copper scenario, only the environ- mental impact to human toxicity was significant. Climate change, terrestrial acidification, photochemical oxidant forma- tion, particulate matter formation, fossil depletion, and fresh- water and marine ecotoxicity had minor contributions and all the other impact categories could be disregarded. To obtain an improved understanding of the contributions of the dominant pollutants to the aforementioned major impact categories, the contributions of the key substances to these cat- egories were presented in Fig. 3 . In both scenarios, the contri- bution of carbon dioxide to climate change was the highest, followed by methane. Mercury and arsenic emissions contrib- uted most to human toxicity in the refined and reclaimed copper scenarios, respectively. The contribution of copper emission to water was the highest for freshwater and marine ecotoxicity in the refined copper industry, and the use of copper was the sole factor of metal depletion. For the reclaimed copper scenario, bromine, nickel, and copper emissions to water contributed the most to freshwater and marine ecotoxicity, whereas copper and arsenic emission to air played another dominant role in marine ecotoxicity. The dominant substances that cause metal deple- tion included copper, iron, and nickel. Compared with the reclaimed copper industry where coal and oil similarly contrib- uted to fossil depletion, coal played a dominant role in fossil depletion in the refined copper scenario. Figure 4 shows the key processes in the production of re- fined and reclaimed copper and their contributions to the 18 midpoint environmental categories. In both scenarios, direct emission and electricity were important contributors for cate- gories such as climate change, terrestrial acidification, marine eutrophication, human toxicity, photochemical oxidant forma- tion, particulate matter formation, and water depletion. Copper mine and crude copper used during the production of refined copper were the main contributors to freshwater ecotoxicity, marine ecotoxicity, agriculture land occupation, urban land oc- cupation, and metal depletion. Heavy fuel oil consumption dur- ing the reclaimed copper production contributed to most cate- gories except for climate change, marine eutrophication, and human toxicity. Furthermore, organic chemicals played an im- portant role in the freshwater eutrophication, terrestrial ecotoxicity, ionizing radiation, agriculture land occupation, wa- ter depletion, metal depletion, and fossil depletion categories during the production of reclaimed copper. 3.2 Sensitivity analysis Table 4 presents the sensitivity analysis results. For the refined copper scenario, the effect of the variation of electricity con- sumption was the highest on climate change and fossil deple- tion in which a 5% electricity reduction could decrease 40.57 kg CO 2 eq and 9.75 kg oil eq. The effect of the changes of direct emission and copper mines was the highest in the Int J Life Cycle Assess human toxicity and rest categories, respectively. For the climate change category, the midpoint values were 1.91 × 10 3 and 688.62 kg CO 2 eq, and the GSD 2 values were 1.24 and 1.21 for refined and reclaimed copper, respective- ly. These results mean that a 95% confidence interval corre- sponds to integration over the climate change score range from 1.54 × 10 3 to 2.39 × 10 3 kg CO 2 eq and 569.11 to 833.23 kg CO 2 eq for refined and reclaimed copper, respectively. The probability of refined copper or reclaimed copper was 100%, thereby indi- cating that the climate change score of the refined copper scenar- io is higher than that of the reclaimed copper scenario. The initial amount of copper was 1.04 and 1.01 tons for per ton copper output. This result indicated that the loss rate was 3.29% for the refined copper. The lost copper mass may be attributed to the limitations related to the missing inventory and measurement error problems. For the rest elements, a similar analogy can be made with the results shown in Table 6 . Conclusively, more than 94% elements were involved, thereby indicating that the inventory presented in this study is within a reasonable range. The aforementioned results indicate that the reclaimed cop- per scenario represented 59 to 99% environmental benefits in most key categories except for human toxicity, in which a similar environmental burden was observed (see Tables 4 and 5 ) because of the direct atmospheric arsenic emission during copper recycling stage. In 2013, copper recycling rate (22.8%, China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association 2014 ) was higher than that reported in Japan (16.7%; World Metal Statistics Yearbook 2013 ), USA (3.8%; World Metal Statistics Yearbook 2013 ), and Russia (14.9%; World Metal Statistics Yearbook 2013 ) but lower than that reported in Germany (29.4%, World Metal Statistics Yearbook 2013 ). If 1% copper recycling rate and arsenic controlling rate are improved, ap- proximately 0.3, 1.4, and 0.3% environmental impacts in the climate change, metal depletion, and fossil depletion catego- ries can be reduced. For the refinery and reclaimed copper scenarios, approximately 0.2 and 0.9% human toxicity burden can be reduced, respectively. In addition, the arsenic concen- trations emitted from the refined copper smelting stage pre- sented in this study (0.34 g/t) are significantly lower than those reported by the European database (2.0 - 32.5 g/t; Process ID: E I 3 C Q U N I 0 0 0 0 6 4 0 1 5 2 0 2 3 7 4 ; E I 3 A R U N I 00011519603682; Ecoinvent center 2015 ). By contrast, the arsenic concentrations presented in the reclaimed copper sce- nario (4.0 g/t) are significantly higher than those shown in the European database (3.5 × 10 − 3 - 2.0 g/t; Process ID: Standard 000034454913626; Standard 000034454913627; Ecoinvent center 2015 ). This result indicated that the improvement po- tential for atmospheric arsenic control in the reclaimed copper industry in China was high. To improve the air quality in China, the Chinese government implemented a new limit on arsenic emission for the reclaimed copper plants on July 1, 2015 (GB 31574- 2015 ). The required upper limit of arsenic and its compounds is 0.4 mg/m 3 , which is lower than the concentration (0.14 - 3.0 mg/m 3 ) presented in this study. If the arsenic emission from the reclaimed copper scenario is the same with that from the refined scenario, then approxi- mately 75% environmental benefit can be achieved in the human toxicity category. The re- sults indicated that the environmental impacts for refined cop- per production were mainly generated from the coal mining stage, which is consistent with the results presented in the current study (Figs. 2 and 4 and Table 4 ). Memary et al. ( 2012 ) developed a time-series LCA for copper mining and smelting in Australia since the 1940. Results showed that global warming potential for per ton copper production ranged from approximately 2.5 to 8.5 t-CO 2 eq. Similarly, Reuter et al. ( 2015 ) reported that the global warming potential score for copper production in Europe was ranged from approximately 2.6 to 5.6 t-CO 2 eq/t-copper, which was higher than the result (1.9 t-CO 2 eq/t-copper) presented in the current study. However, the values in the primary energy demand and global warming impact for the refined copper production were approximately 1.5 to 2 times higher than those in European ecoinvent database (i.e., Process ID: EI3CQUNI 000064015202374; EI3ARUNI 00011519603682; Ecoinvent center 2015 ) because of the varying of energy structure between Europe and China, the overuse of energy in China, and the missing inventory of carbon dioxide emis- sions in the European database. Coal-based electricity gener- ation is used in this study because coal plays an important role in China ' s energy structure (National Bureau of Statistic of China 2015 ). If the current hydropower share rate (17%, National Bureau of Statistic of China 2015 ) is considered in this study, approximately 7 and 14% of the primary energy demand and global warming impacts, respectively, can be reduced. Thus, copper production with clean energy, such as hydropower, is crucial to reduce the overall environmental burden. However, copper products are currently produced in Shandong, Henan, Jiangsu, Anhui, and Jiangxi with a relative- ly low hydroelectricity share rate (China Nonferrous Metals Industry Yearbook 2015 ; China Energy Statistical Yearbook 2014 ). Thus, the relocation of the copper industry near areas with abundant clean energy sources is highly recommended. 4 Conclusions This research evaluated the environmental impact and the im- provement potentials of the copper production in China by conducting LCA. Uncertainty analysis is also performed to increase the reliability of this study. The main conclusions drawn from the present study are: & The emissions of carbon dioxide, mercury, arsenic, and copper, use of coal and oil, and mining copper ore were the most significant contributors to the overall environ- mental burden. & The direct emission level of arsenic generated by the reclaimed copper industry in China is significantly higher than that of the Europe technologies. & Compared with the refined copper scenario, approximate- ly 59 to 99% environmental benefits in each key category will be achieved for the reclaimed copper scenario. & Efficient methods to reduce the overall environmental im- pact of copper production are increasing the direct heavy metal emissions in air and water, the recycling rate of copper, electricity consumption efficiency, the utilization rate of clean energy sources, and the efficiency of copper ore mining and consumption. The results presented in this study can potentially expand the life cycle inventory database of copper production in China, as well as provide useful information for policy- makers in China in making decisions regarding the eco-de- sign, management, education, policy making, and problem rectification of the copper industry. However, other technolo- gies (e.g., flash smelting, flash converting, oxygen bottom/ side blowing melting, Baiyin copper smelting, copper hydro- metallurgy, and blast furnace smelting) should be continued to be studied. Additionally, the economic and social impacts on the copper industries in China should be further addressed for more sustainable development. Further research on this area will be conducted by our research group.
